Your house in Riverdale, and what we would do with it

Most houses around Riverdale went up in the 1950s. Housing that age normally still has its original trim, and that trim is already carrying a lot of paint. It is the reason two painters can look at the same Riverdale house and hand you very different numbers. One of them has priced the preparation and one of them has not.

In Riverdale that mostly means drywall repair and interior painting, with exterior painting on the same visit often enough that splitting them wastes everyone's time. We are 11.1 straight-line miles away at 7900 W. 83rd St. in Bridgeview.

  • Can we do your job? Almost certainly. In Riverdale it is drywall repair and interior painting most weeks, plus the drywall, plaster and carpentry that goes underneath both.
  • What will it cost? There is no price list on this site, because there is no honest local one to publish yet. Every job is quoted after we walk it. What moves the number on a Riverdale house is condition rather than size: what has to come off or be made good in Riverdale before anything new goes on.
  • What usually needs doing first? In Riverdale it is normally the making-good: plaster that has opened up, windows painted shut, and trim that has lost its edge under old coats.
  • When can you come? We are 11.1 straight-line miles out, and travel is not a hidden line on a quote from us. Depends on the job. Riverdale is a genuine drive, so a full interior or a whole exterior is straightforward to schedule and one small patch on its own may not be. You will be told which.

Why two quotes for the same Riverdale house come out different

Masonry walls change the exterior job completely. On 15.4 percent prewar stock and a 1957 median, there is very little painted wall outside: the work is the porch, the cornice, the soffit, the fascia, the garage surround and the sash. All of it is detail, most of it is off a ladder, and none of it is quotable from a photograph. The 2,053 to 1,819 split between owning and renting in Riverdale means the same street can want two different things. A contractor who prices both the same way is wrong about one of them.

What an estimate here has to account for

  • Distance, stated. Riverdale is 11.1 straight-line miles from the shop. Travel to Riverdale is not a hidden line item on this site and it should not be one on a written quote either.
  • Containment, not just paint. 88.8 percent of housing in Riverdale was built before 1980, so on most addresses here the lead-safe setup and the cleanup are part of the job and part of the hours.
  • Plaster as well as drywall. 15.4 percent of Riverdale is prewar. Plaster cracks along the lath and comes back if it is only filled, so wall repair is a different line from wall painting.
  • Setup does not shrink with the room. The median unit here is 5 rooms. Masking, cutting in and cleanup cost the same in a small room as a large one, so a flat per-room rate is usually wrong in one direction or the other.

What the housing here is likely made of

Most of it is brick bungalow, Cape Cod and early ranch. The walls are masonry, so exterior paint concentrates in trim, soffit, fascia, garage surround and doors. Riverdale interiors are trim-heavy for their square footage.

It is read off exactly two things: the 1957 median build year, and the split between 54.3 percent detached houses, 8.2 percent attached homes and 35.9 percent in buildings of two units or more.

Lead paint: the short version for Riverdale

Old paint is the thing to know about here. Riverdale is largely 1950s housing, and anything painted before 1978 may have lead in the layers underneath. It is handled rather than avoided: the room is closed off, the dust is contained while the work happens, and the site is cleaned to a set standard before anyone leaves.

The practical content of it is dust. Where paint in a Riverdale room gets disturbed past about six square feet, twenty outside, or wherever a window comes out, the work has to be contained and cleaned to a standard. That is time at both ends of the job, and it is why an honest quote on 2,053 homes worth of 1957-median housing reads longer than a fast one.

None of it is graded at the town line. The rule attaches to a build year and to the work being done, so the number worth checking is the one on your own deed in Riverdale.

The Census publishes a pre-1980 bucket rather than a pre-1978 one, and on that measure 88.8 percent of the housing sits on the older side of the line in Riverdale. That puts most of the housing inside the federal lead-safe renovation rule, which attaches to pre-1978 homes and to work that disturbs the paint on them. In Illinois it is administered by EPA rather than by a state agency.

None of that is a reason to leave a Riverdale house unpainted. It is a reason to know what the setup looks like before anyone opens a sander, and to hear it from the person doing the work rather than from a website.

Not proportionally, no. The median unit in Riverdale is 5 rooms, and a small room still needs the same masking, the same cutting in and the same cleanup as a large one. What falls is the roller time, which is the cheapest part of the day. Anyone quoting a flat per-room rate on small rooms is either guessing high or about to be disappointed.
